utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-00-41-PT, the Prosecutor versus Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Counsel Mark Harmon, Fergal Gaynor, and Donnica Henry-Frijlink for the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jonjic. Now I'm turning to Mr. Ljubicic. Can you hear me in a language that you understand? It seems that there is a slight problem. I would like the usher to provide some assistance. Okay. Good afternoon, Mr. Ljubicic. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Translate. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to intervene once again. Okay. Good afternoon, Mr. Ljubicic. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You can sit down. Today's hearing -- is there a problem, Mr. Harhoff?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just the answer provided by the accused was not translated into English but we got it on the French channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Because I had the translation in French. There seems to be a problem. Okay. Very well. Thank you. If there is no problem, then we can start. Let me tell you first that this -- today's hearing was set for today but it was set beyond the time frame provided for by the Rules. But the Judges of the Chamber and myself received confirmation, both from Mr. Ljubicic and from the Prosecution that it was in the interest of justice to go beyond the time frame provided by the Rules for today's Status Conference. So I complied with the request from the parties following the agreement expressed by Mr. Ljubicic when setting today's hearing for this Status Conference. I'd like to remind the parties that following the last Status Conference held in this case, as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, I had come to the conclusion that the case, or rather, that the pre-trial stage had been completed, and I drew up the report provided for by the Rules and I sent the report to the Chamber and to the President of the Tribunal for him to take the necessary steps in the best interest of justice within this Tribunal. Let me explain what I'm talking about. The idea is to set a date possible -- probable date for the opening of the trial in this case within the framework of the work of the Tribunal. This being said, first of all I want to make sure that Mr. Ljubicic has no complaints regarding his health. Mr. Ljubicic, would you like us to move into private session to deal with that issue or are you ready to answer in open session without us going into private session? You have the choice. You can decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not necessary to move into a closed session as far as I and my health are concerned. My health condition is good. I have no complaints regarding my conditions of detention. I have no complaints about the personnel in the Detention Unit. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm glad to hear this. Now I would like to turn to the parties to ask if anybody wants to raise any issue. But before that, I would like to say a few words about a motion that is still pending before the Trial Chamber. I am talking about the Defence motion for provisional release. We received a response of the latest reply or response from the Defence on the 8th of November, 2004. In that response the Defence replies to the submissions made by the Prosecution on the 1st of November. And in its submissions, the Prosecution reiterates its position and states that it is against the provisional release of the accused. I can tell the parties that a decision will probably be taken by the Trial Chamber after careful consideration of the submissions of the parties. If the parties want to add anything to their previous submissions, I will be glad to listen to them. Does the Prosecution want to add anything to their -- to the previous submissions? Mr. Harmon, would you like add anything to your submissions of the 1st of November, 2004? Is there anything else you would like to add or do you maintain your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We maintain our position, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Jonjic, is there anything else you would like to add to your previous submissions and to what was explained by Mr. Ljubicic in an annex to your reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Defence does not have anything further to add. And for reasons of judicial economy, we're not going to repeat the arguments set out in our written submission. However, let me correct a mistake done by Defence's translator. In the statement of the 3rd of November, in the translation of that statement under 2, at the very top of page 10 of the entire submission, instead of "the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina" should read "the Government of the Republic of Croatia." So it is a mistake committed by the Defence. I just wanted to advise the Chamber of this error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. There's no problem. But I would like you to read out yourself the text in Serbian for it to be -- for the transcript to reflect what you've just said. So you are talking about paragraph number 2, aren't you? Paragraph number 2 of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, paragraph 2 of the statement, Your Honour, which reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Prosecutor submits that the Defence has failed to submit to warranties of the Federation of BH." I wish to remind the Chamber that in their first request the Defence has received the warranties of the Republic of Croatia. That same government, after someone's intervention, not knowing whose intervention, after an argument, withdrew their guarantees. That is the original text. That is how it should have been translated. However, the error was committed and that's why we had the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I understand. Thank you very much. Well, let's look at the position of the Defence. What are the guarantees we are dealing -- talking about here? You said that the Government of Croatia at first said -- provided guarantees but then decided to withdraw these guarantees. Are you going to contact the government to ask for further guarantees or new guarantees? Or do you think -- or how do you think we should go about this issue? Because my second question is the following, and I'm going also to turn to the Prosecution for that matter. My second question is that the issue is that it's absolutely essential for a government to provide guarantees when it comes to a provisional release. So can you please answer my first question, which is the following: Do you intend to ask a government, whether the Croatian government or the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you intend to ask a government for guarantees?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is perfectly aware of the fact that the guarantees of a government is not a precondition for a provisional release, at least not according to the wording of the Rules. However, the case law of this Tribunal demonstrates that a motion without such guarantees does not have good chances of succeeding. That is why the Defence, before they submitted their motion for provisional release in the first half of 2002, which motion was rejected in a decision of this Chamber on the 2nd of August, 2002, did contact the government of the Republic of Croatia, which government on that occasion did issue guarantees which were attached to the motion for provisional release. After that, the government withdrew its guarantees, which was, of course, attached in the Prosecution's response to our motion. When we now speak about the guarantees which were issued and then withdrawn in our present motion, we are referring to the guarantees which were first issued and then withdrawn in April and May 2002, respectively. The Defence did contact the relevant governments and we received oral assurances from ministers of both governments, the justice minister of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and justice minister of the Republic of Croatia, who promised that such guarantees would be issued in a written form shortly. The same statements and the same promises were given to Mr. Ljubicic when the representatives of these governments paid him a visit in the Detention Unit. However, despite several appeals from the Defence, the governments did not fulfill their promise. After that, Mr. Ljubicic, as you can see from the statement of the 3rd of November, 2004, requested me to withdraw my application, my request, because he believed the behaviour of both governments to constitute an obstacle -- obstruction of his Defence, which has been going on for quite some time, for several years, and which can be seen also from the fact that many of the necessary documents have been denied to him. And that is why he had to address himself to this Honourable Chamber, who then issued orders for the production of documents. Now, this was a brief procedural overview and you have the statement of Mr. Ljubicic, I believe, in front of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand very well. You've already -- you've also explained that according to the case law of the Tribunal, guarantees are necessary and requested. I can believe that Mr. Ljubicic made the decision of not asking for guarantees, not asking these governments for guarantees, but you as a Defence counsel should advise and should act in the best interest of Mr. Ljubicic. And if you believe that some steps must be taken in order to turn these orally -- oral guarantees into written and official guarantees, if you can do that, I think it is your duty to do so even if Mr. Ljubicic for one reason or another believes that he doesn't need to ask for these guarantees. If you yourself believe that it is possible to explore this -- these avenues, I then believe that it is your duty as a professional first of all to advise Mr. Ljubicic on that matter, and secondly to act in his -- in the interest of justice. I would even go as far as saying in the interest of justice. In your opinion, would further steps be successful or do you share the position of Mr. Ljubicic who says that they will never provide these guarantees and I do not want these guarantees? I would like to hear what you yourself as a professional think about this, as a professional entrusted with the Defence of Mr. Ljubicic. I would like to know what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do share your view and your assessment of the need for me to act as a professional counsel. And in light of that, I can state that despite -- or rather, notwithstanding the request of Mr. Ljubicic to withdraw the application from both governments, I got in touch with the -- these governments once again and I tried to explain to them that the position of my defendant is such that he wished this application to be withdrawn. That is to say, I advised them of this protest of my defendant. However, this remained without a reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting, but just a point of detail: Do you remember when you started doing all this, started explaining to the government that it was absolutely essential for the government to say what it -- what was -- what its position was? It was after the 3rd of November, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the original applications were sent to the governments in April this year. They have been repeated on several occasions, and my last intervention was made on the same day when I received from Mr. Ljubicic by fax from the Detention Unit this statement which is annexed to the documents that you have. So my last attempt was after he made his statement in November 2004. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what are you saying? Is it on the 3rd or around that date, on the 3rd of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 3rd of November for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you sent that application in writing? It was a written application?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, as I did every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, of course, an official, formal application, but I believe that there are also official contacts that could speed up the entire proceedings or enable you to gain more information. What is the attitude of the administration? Are they reluctant or is this delay due to the administrative procedures or -- in your opinion, what is the situation? Are you expecting a response within two weeks or one month?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think it's a matter of a routine, or rather the normal delays. Because once again, I think it was in July this year, in my attempt to obtain these guarantees I talked to the chief of police in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose consent is a precondition, a prerequisite, for the government to issue such guarantees. And it was the chief of police who on that occasion told me that as far as he was concerned there was no obstacle whatsoever for such guarantees to be issued and that he had written a letter to that effect to the minister of justice. My request for this letter to be provided to me was refused. He explained that it was a matter of internal communication between different government bodies, but he said that the reference to this letter would be contained in the guarantees which were to be provided to me by the government. However, as I have indicated, I haven't a response to this date from the government. I cannot rule out the possibility that should I perhaps try once again, I might be -- I would be successful this time. However, I have good reasons for being skeptical. The Defence would by all means prefer to have the guarantees which would facilitate their position, but this is something out of our ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, you've sent your application to the government of the federation. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. Because in the motion for provisional release, the place of residence of Mr. Ljubicic, in case the motion is granted, is Mostar, where his family lives. And Mostar being in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was necessary to apply for these guarantees to the government of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question: You -- not excluding the possibility of a positive response possibly, if necessary steps are taken in that direction. I'd like to explore all avenues open to us and try to find out everything that will help the Chamber to rule within the framework of the case law. You mentioned the case law yourself, and according to the case law, a number of prerequisites are set. So even if there's the slightest chance of succeeding, I think it's worth the effort, it's worth trying. I don't know if you're -- you share my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand what you're trying to say and I do share your view. However, even after on the 3rd of November, 2004, Mr. Ljubicic gave me his statement, I did not withdraw my application for guarantees which had been sent to the government. So this application is still pending. There has been no decision on the application. I can perhaps try once again to obtain such guarantees. And if the Chamber can wait with a decision on the motion, I could perhaps try once again to obtain the guarantees from the government and provide the Chamber with the guarantees as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a step that is necessary in order to enable the Chamber to be in the best possible position to rule on that motion. And I believe that it is necessary for you to make that effort. And I'm expecting you to inform the Chamber as early as possible in that sense. Thank you very much, Mr. Jonjic. Now I'm turning to the Prosecution, to Mr. Harmon. I always enjoy the way the logic -- the legal logic applied by Mr. Harmon -- legal reasoning. According to you, Mr. Harmon, how should one interpret Rule 65? I'm talking about 65(B) and (C). According to the Rules, is it absolutely necessary for the government of the country - I'm quoting Rule 65(B) - "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only after giving the host country and the state to which the accused seeks to be released the opportunity to be heard." And then Rule 65(C): "The Trial Chamber may impose conditions upon the release of the accused as it may determine appropriate, including the execution of a bail bond and the observance of such conditions as are necessary to ensure the presence of the accused for trial and the protection of others." Mr. Harmon, I would like to know what is your point of view about this matter, notwithstanding the case law, very consistent case law, of the Tribunal so far. Do you believe that it is necessary, on top of the fact that we need to hear the authorities of the state where the accused wants to be released, so beyond that, beyond having the state heard, is it also absolutely necessary for that state to provide guarantees? Is it an obligation? Is it a legal obligation? Or is it something that comes under the discretion of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a very good question and one which I can provide you a more comprehensive answer when I have the opportunity to research the specific question you've asked me. I don't have the answer at hand. But I can say, Your Honour, a number of things. I do believe that under (B) it is required that the host country be given the opportunity to be heard. Furthermore, that the state, in this case Bosnia and Herzegovina, be given an opportunity to be heard. And further, the Court has to be satisfied that the accused will appear at trial and that he will not pose any danger to any victim witness or other person. Now, on the issue of the guarantee, there have been two guarantees sought, one from Croatia. We are familiar with the history of that; that has been outlined in previous pleadings, in our pleading as well. Croatia was the initial country where Mr. Ljubicic sought his release. And that has already been litigated and we know the status of that particular guarantee. Mr. Jonjic has described a rather long effort, an arduous effort to get a guarantee from Bosnia and he has been unsuccessful. That seems, to me, to speak volumes. So there is no guarantee, as the record currently stands, from Bosnia. I think there is a very good reason why a guarantee is a critical element, but not necessarily dispositive, in the Trial Chamber's consideration as to whether to release somebody or not. We do not have a police force in the Tribunal; we have to rely on the states to essentially secure the arrest of people. A state that is not willing to guarantee or make guarantees to this Tribunal makes the Prosecutor's office and a decision of a Trial Chamber to release someone even more vulnerable. It is more reassuring, Your Honour, when a state will say affirmatively, We will make guarantees to ensure that a particular accused will appear in all proceedings before this institution as required. Absent such a guarantee, Your Honour, we have the prospect of losing an accused forever. And as the Court well knows, there have been people who have been indicted in this institution many, many, many years ago who remain fugitives. That's perhaps our biggest fear in these situations. Right now, Mr. Ljubicic is in custody. He's here, he's been here for three years. He has asked for an expeditious trial. We support his request to be tried. Our view - and I know this is not directly in response to your question - our view is that we would encourage, rather than a release of Mr. Ljubicic which exposes the Tribunal to the possibility that Mr. Ljubicic could disappear, we support a different proposition and that is to give Mr. Ljubicic his trial and to do so as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand perfectly what you're saying. But let me submit to you a hypothesis, the following: The relation between a guarantee and the obligation to cooperate. In other words, if a state does not provide a formal guarantee, that state is nonetheless obligated to cooperate with the Tribunal. That is to say, if the Tribunal requests the -- from the local police that they lead the accused or take the accused to the Tribunal, then the state in question is forced -- has the obligation to comply, because it is under the obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal. I'm raising this issue because, as Mr. Jonjic quite rightly pointed out, if we look at the case law of the Tribunal, it's what you said. It's in the direction that you pointed out yourself. The Tribunal doesn't have a police force, the Tribunal depends on the authorities, judicial authorities and other types of authorities of other countries. But I'm only raising the issue as an hypothesis, something that might be envisaged. In any case, we'll wait for the outcome of the applications that Mr. Jonjic is going to submit. He told us so himself, he's going to submit these applications to the relevant authorities of the confederation. But nonetheless, for things to be as clear as possible, I would like you to submit your point of view and explain to us how you see the interaction of Rule 65(B) and 65(C) related to the conditions that might be set, including the execution of a bail bond. This -- these two paragraphs could be interpreted in a different way. That could be applied to this case and maybe to other cases before the Tribunal. I'm looking forward to reading your submissions, because I like reading your submissions as much as I like listening to you. And I would be grateful if you could find the time to draw up submissions on that particular matter. Thank you very much in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We'll -- thank you very much, Your Honour, we will submit written submission on the points we've raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now I'd like to give the floor to Mr. Ljubicic. I'd like to ask him if he wants to address the Chamber. I can see that you've prepared some sort of memo that you have in front of you. You can say whatever you like. I'm all ears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not going to say much and I'm probably not going to say anything new, anything that my counsel or myself have not said on a previous occasion. Let me just repeat once again because I think it wouldn't be amiss to hear certain things several times. I am perfectly aware of this one black stain that I have on my name, and that is the 16th of April, 1993. No one needed police forces to bring me here, police force in Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina. I knocked on their door, I told them who I was three days after I learned that the indictment had been issued by this Tribunal. No police is going to be necessary for anyone, Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina, should I be provisionally released, notwithstanding the decision of the Trial Chamber. Now, I'm talking on the assumption that the motion will be granted, because that stain that I have, I know that it is not as dark as some people here have tried to present it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you, but I'm reading the following in the transcript. "[In English] ... that I have on my name, and that is the 16th of April, 1993." [Interpretation] Is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am charged for the events that took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I am saying this, that is why I mentioned that date. My past can be checked, can be verified by anyone else. They will never realise -- they will never find that I was a criminal or that I had any problems with law. My participation in the events will be finally disclosed in this trial and the facts will be assessed. However, from what I was able to understand from the judgements that I have read from this Tribunal, these facts cannot be reproached to me. I am not going to disappear. I am -- I intend to respect every decision issued by the Tribunal and I intend to abide by the orders of the Tribunal and the police should I be provisionally released. I have been in detention for three years and I do not know when the trial is going to take place. One more sentence related to the guarantees that we requested from the governments of Croatia and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have to say openly that my counsel and myself, we haven't made any public announcements, any public comments. However, promises were made and then promises were not kept. And this is why I said -- it is because of these obstructions of my Defence and my counsel that I was offended. And I said that I no longer needed any guarantees. I didn't need the persons who were obstructing my Defence to issue any kind of guarantees for myself. At any rate, I support what has been indicated by my counsel, Mr. Jonjic. He has warned me of the necessity to provide guarantees. And if they are truly important, we will try to obtain them once again. But as far as I'm concerned, in my personal opinion, they do not mean a thing. What I think is important is what I declare to you, Your Honour, and what I say publicly before this Chamber, notwithstanding the guarantees whether they will be eventually issued or not. And I commit myself to abide by any order, any decision that you intend to order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ljubicic. I believe that nonetheless we should proceed as Mr. Jonjic said he would proceed. I think that it is in your best interest for an application to be made and an application that would probably be granted, application for guarantees that were promised to you before, even if it was only orally. And I believe that very quickly we will hear from Mr. Jonjic who will tell us what was the outcome of the application. This being said, is there any other issue that the parties would like to raise? The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, is there anything else you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, the Defence doesn't have anything to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This being said, the hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: at 3.49 p.m.
